notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1270.tmp1270.opp-lat: 'Relutus' is read as relatus, 'carried back', and 'egectus' as effectus. Stray edition numbers inside the text (39, 19) are left out.
A stray page number (308) inside the text is left out.
'quadringinta' is taken as a late spelling of 'quadraginta', forty, to match the forty days and the palm leaves 'for forty days'; the classical form would mean four hundred.
'olei guttura' is corrupt as printed; it is taken as a flask (guttus) of oil. The misprints 'eum femina', 'incantalionis' and 'operativnem' are read as cum femina, incantationis and operationem.

nodes.text: CHAP. VIII. — So, carried back, he remained alone again as was his custom; and he could not stand because of his fresh wounds, but praying prostrate, after the prayer he said in a clear voice: Here I am, I, Antony; I do not flee your contests; even if you make them greater, nothing shall separate me from the love of Christ (Rom. 8). And he sang psalms, saying: Though camps be set against me, my heart shall not fear (Ps. 26). As he said such things, the devil, enemy of the good, amazed that after so many blows he had dared to return, gathered his hounds and, tearing at himself in his own fury, said: You see that, overcome neither by the spirit of fornication nor by the pains of the body, he even boldly provokes us. Seize every weapon; he must be attacked by us more fiercely. Let him feel it, let him feel it. He must learn whom he is provoking. He spoke, and at the voice of the one urging them on the crowd of listeners agreed, for the devil has countless arts of doing harm. So a sudden noise crashed out, so that the place was shaken to its foundations and the walls were laid open, and a manifold crowd of demons poured out from there; for, putting on the forms of beasts and of serpents, they at once filled the whole place with phantoms of lions, bulls, wolves, asps, serpents, scorpions, and also of leopards and bears. And each of these raged according to its own nature. The lion roared, wanting to kill; the bull threatened with bellowing and horns; the serpent resounded with hissing; the wolves hurled their rushes at him; the leopard with its mottled colours displayed the varied cunning of its maker. Savage were the faces of all, and dreadful to hear their bristling voices. Antony, scourged and pierced, felt the harsher pains of the body, but undaunted he held out with a watchful mind. And though the wounds of his flesh forced out a groan, yet remaining the same in mind, as though he were mocking his enemies, he said: If you had any strength, one of you would be enough for the battle; but since you are broken, the Lord having sapped your strength, you try to bring terror by numbers, when this itself is a sign of weakness, that you put on the forms of irrational beasts. And again, full of confidence, he said: If you have any power, if the Lord has given you power over me, here I am, ready: devour what has been granted. But if you cannot, why do you strive in vain? For the sign of the cross and faith toward the Lord are an impregnable wall for us. Threatening much against holy Antony, they gnashed their teeth, because no effect followed their assaults, but rather, quite the contrary, only mockery [of themselves] came of it.

43. This too was confirmed to us as true about him by those who heard it from his own mouth: that once, at night, a demon in the guise of a monk knocked at the door of his cell, saying: Get up, Abba Macarius, and let us go to the assembly, where the brothers are gathering for the vigils (Rufinus, bk. 2, ch. 29, word for word). But he, filled with the grace of God, could not be deceived; for he understood that it was the devil's deceit, and said: O liar and enemy of the truth, what fellowship, what partnership do you have with the assembly and gathering of the saints? But he said: Do you not know, then, Macarius, that no assembly is held without us, nor any gathering of monks? Come, then, and you will see our work there. Holy Macarius said: The Lord rebuke you, unclean demon (Epistle of Jude). And turning to prayer, he asked the Lord to show him whether what the demon had boasted was true. So he went to the assembly, where the vigils were already being celebrated by the brothers, and again in prayer he besought the Lord to show him the truth of this word; and behold, he sees what seemed to be little black Ethiopian boys running about here and there through the whole church, and being carried along as if flying. These Ethiopian boys, running about, played tricks on each of the brothers as they stood in prayer and sang psalms; and if they pressed anyone's eyes with two little fingers, he at once fell asleep; and if they put a finger into anyone's mouth, they made him yawn. Likewise, after the psalm, when the brothers had thrown themselves down to pray, they ran round to each one again; before one lying in prayer they turned themselves as it were into the form of a woman, before another they appeared as if building and carrying something, or doing all sorts of different things; and whatever the demons, as if at play, had shaped, those men at prayer turned over there in the thoughts of their hearts. By some of the brothers, however, as soon as they began to do any of these things, they were driven back as if by force and flung headlong down, so that they did not dare even to stand or pass before them; but on others they even played upon their necks and backs. When holy Macarius saw this, he groaned deeply and, pouring out tears to God, said: Look, Lord, and do not keep silent, and do not be still, O God; but arise, and let your enemies be scattered and flee from your face, for our soul is filled with illusions (Psalms 82, 87). After the prayer, to test the truth, he called aside each of the brothers before whose faces he had seen the demons playing in different guises and various images, and asked them whether during prayer they had had thoughts of building, or of making a journey, or of other different things, which he had seen pictured for each of them by the demons; and each of them confessed that the thoughts had been in his heart just as he charged. And then it was truly understood that all the evil, superfluous and vain thoughts which anyone conceives in his heart, whether while singing psalms or at the time of dreams or of prayers, come about through the illusion and prompting of demons. For by those who guard their heart with all vigilance in the fear and love of the Lord, those dark Ethiopians and the thoughts they send out are driven back; for a mind joined to Christ, and especially intent at the time of prayer, takes in nothing evil and nothing superfluous.

23. A man once came to Scetis to become a monk. He also brought his son, newly weaned. When the son had become a young man, demons began to attack and tempt him. And he said to his father: I am going back to the world, because I cannot endure the desires of the flesh. His father comforted him. Then the young man said: I can no longer endure it, father; let me go back to the world. His father said to him: Listen to me, son, once more: take forty loaves and palm leaves for forty days, and go into the inner desert, and stay there forty days, and the will of God will be done. Obeying his father, he got up and went into the desert, and stayed there, working and making plaits of dry palm and eating dry bread. And when he had stayed there quietly for twenty days, behold, he saw a work of the devil coming upon him; and there stood before him what seemed an Ethiopian woman, stinking and foul to look at, so that he could not bear her stench, and he thrust her away from him. And she said to him: I am she who appears sweet in the hearts of men; but because of your obedience and the labour you endure, God has not permitted me to seduce you, but I have made my stench known to you. He got up and, giving thanks to God, came to his father and said to him: I no longer want to go to the world, father. For I have seen the working of the devil and his stench. His father too had known of this very thing, and said to him: If you had stayed forty days and kept my command to the end, you would have seen greater things.

Cronius also related that on that night the great Antony had told them this: I, he said, had prayed for a whole year that the place of the righteous and of sinners might be revealed to me (above, bk. 1, in the Life of St Antony, ch. 38; Paschasius, ch. 19, no. 4). And I saw a very tall black giant, who reached right up to the clouds, and he had his hands stretched out right up to heaven; and below him was a lake that equalled the sea in size. I also saw souls flying upward like birds; and whichever flew over his hands and head were kept safe by angels, but those that were struck by his hands fell into the lake. Then a voice came to me, which said: The souls you see that have flown over the giant's head and his hands are the souls of the righteous, which are kept by angels in paradise; but those that are struck by the hands of the black one are plunged into hell. These are the ones that were drawn by the will of the flesh, and followed hatred and the desire to repay injury.

A certain woman of noble birth, who bore the yoke of marriage together with a dissolute husband, came to that blessed man, bewailing her own misfortune. For she said that her husband, captivated by his intimacy with a concubine, had been bewitched by certain magical tricks, and hated her, who was joined to him in lawful marriage. The woman said this standing before the doors of the forecourt; for that is how he used to speak with a woman: he never admitted any woman within his doors. Then, taking pity on the wailing woman, he abolished the working of the spell by prayer; and when he had sanctified with divine invocation a flask of oil she had brought, he ordered that she be anointed with it. When the woman had carried out these instructions, she turned her husband's love toward herself, and persuaded him to choose the lawful bed instead of the unlawful one.
